newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Poll shows GST a vote winner for Australia govt.
newsitem.headline: Poll shows GST a vote winner for Australia govt.

text.p: A goods-and-services tax (GST) would be a vote winner if Australia's Liberal-National coalition government adopted it as a policy for the next election, according to an opinion poll released on Monday.

The Bulletin newsweekly's Morgan poll showed 59 percent of the voters it surveyed now favoured a GST, compared with 56 percent a year ago. Those who opposed it had dropped to 31 percent from 37 percent a year earlier.
"The government clearly has received a positive public response by putting the GST on the agenda for the next election," pollster Gary Morgan said.
Morgan said it was significant that 14 percent of Labor opposition supporters said they would switch to the coalition government because it favoured a GST.
Among Coalition voters, only six percent would defect to the Labor Party because of their dislike of the GST.
The poll also showed a considerable jump in support for the government, which could be attributed to the belief that a GST may be back on the agenda, he said.
Prime Minister John Howard said last week that open debate on taxation reform was needed in Australia.
The poll, taken on May 21 and 22, showed that the coalition would receive 55 percent of the vote on a two-party preferred basis, compared with 51.5 percent a week earlier.
Support for the opposition, which continues to oppose a GST, fell to 45 percent from 48.5 percent over the same period.

"Given the hypothetical situation of an election with the GST as the key issue and the two major parties campaigning on opposition sides of the debate, the poll puts the coalition at 52 percent and the Labor Party at 35 percent," Morgan said.
A GST is a consumption tax or value-added tax that is paid by consumers when they buy a good or service.
The Coalition was widely perceived to have lost the 1993 election because of its plans to introduce a GST.
It ousted the 13-year-old Labor administration in March 1996 after dropping the tax and pledging not to introduce a GST in its first term.
But it has not ruled out such a tax in later terms.
